papers.title: Back to Pixels: Lifting Latent Video Diffusion into Pixel Space
papers.authors: Yanke Song, Shuo Chen, Chris Rockwell, Guande He et al.
papers.summary: Frontier video generation models work in a VAE latent space that compresses video in both space and time. This compression made training tractable, but now limits high-resolution, controllable, and interactive generation – doubling resolution quadruples token count, conditions apply to groups of frames rather than individual ones, and each response must wait for the rest of its multi-frame block. We present PixVid, a simple yet effective method that lifts a pretrained latent video model to directly generate every frame in pixel space. PixVid keeps the diffusion transformer and replaces the VAE decoder with a convolutional head that renders its outputs into pixels. We find that predicting clean video rather than velocity, together with a larger noise shift, is key to quality. Finetuned from Wan2.1-14B, PixVid is competitive with the latent baseline within 1.3M training clips. Working framewise in pixels, it generates at 2× higher resolution with the same per-frame token count, keeps depth-conditioned video editing aligned under fast motion, and responds to each action at the next frame. Project page: https://chenshuo20.github.io/PixVid/

papers.title: Unbundling Multimodal Vision Encoding
papers.authors: Ellis Brown, Chris Hoang, Shengyi Qian, Shang-Wen Li et al.
papers.summary: How multimodal language models should encode visual input remains up for debate. Most models use a pretrained vision encoder, while some recent recipes train the encoder from scratch with the language model or remove it entirely. Vision encoders bundle together three design choices: a visual prior from upstream pretraining, dedicated vision capacity, and pre-fusion placement of that capacity (i.e., before the multimodal backbone). Because published models also differ in data, architecture, and compute, comparing them cannot isolate the effect of each choice. We disentangle these choices via a controlled framework where we pretrain all models from scratch on common data and compare them on visual question answering and language benchmarks at matched lifetime compute. We find that the visual prior is not necessary; an encoder trained jointly from scratch is on par with a pretrained one, without a separate training stage. What matters instead is dedicated vision capacity: an encoder-free model trails on visual understanding even when its backbone is enlarged by the encoder's parameter count. Yet that capacity need not precede multimodal fusion, as vision-only modules added in-fusion to early backbone layers perform comparably to a pre-fusion encoder and can lower time to first token. These results also hold across backbone sizes, when encoder pretraining is treated as free, and when starting from a pretrained language model. Overall, our findings favor dedicated vision capacity trained jointly with the backbone and placed early within it.

papers.title: ArchSpace: Recording, Reviewing, and Referencing LLM Architecture Research
papers.authors: Jie Wang, Tong Zhu, JiaHao Kuang, Zhe Xu et al.
papers.summary: Model architecture shapes the scaling behavior, training efficiency, and inference cost of LLMs, making it a central focus of both industry and academia. In industry, teams such as those behind DeepSeek, Qwen, and Kimi routinely introduce architectural innovations, yet public reports rarely document which ideas succeeded, which were abandoned, and why. In academia, limited compute and inconsistent baselines often restrict evaluations to small-scale, single-point comparisons, making it difficult to establish whether improvements hold at larger scales or translate into broader impact. ArchSpace addresses both gaps as a public platform for Recording, Reviewing, and Referencing Architecture Researc: each proposal is recorded with its experiments and reasoning, reviewed by the community, and referenced by later work. To evaluate ideas before costly large-scale training, ArchSpace leverages scaling laws to predict model loss at larger scales from smaller experiments, a practice widely adopted in industry. We provide initial references that make the platform usable: Qwen3.5 and OLMo3 baselines, fitted scaling laws, and a reusable training recipe. Ideas validated through this review can in turn become new baselines, and ArchSpace thereby aims to broaden the range of ideas that shape the next generation of models.

papers.title: TTB: Test-time Baking for Efficient Rendering of Decoder-only View Synthesis Models
papers.authors: Chin-Yang Lin, Ryo Hachiuma, Jaesung Choe, Min-Hung Chen et al.
papers.summary: Decoder-only Large View Synthesis Models (LVSMs) with KV-cache have recently achieved state-of-the-art quality by regressing novel views from neural networks without reconstructing 3D geometry, while Test-Time Training (TTT) layers save computation but sacrifice quality. We propose Test-Time Baking (TTB), a strategy that learns to bake global scene information from cross-view attention into a lightweight MLP, enabling fast and high-fidelity novel-view decoding. The first key is to repurpose the fast-weight MLP of TTT to learn the cross-view attention mapping explicitly from its input-output pairs, rather than replacing attention entirely, achieving the same rendering efficiency as TTT while delivering substantially higher quality. The second key addresses a modality misalignment between context prefilling and novel-view rendering: we disentangle context tokens into camera-only context rendering tokens to serve as TTB input, and context ground-truth tokens with image content to serve as the TTB mapping target, ensuring the baked MLPs are relieved of the modality generalization challenge between context and novel-view processing. Our method achieves up to **23x** rendering speedup with quality on par with the state-of-the-art across several benchmarks. Project page: https://test-time-baking.github.io

papers.title: ProtoVis-Nav: Prototypical Visual Imagination for Visual-Spatial Aligned UAV Navigation
papers.authors: Guangyuan Sui, Yunzhong Hou, Chi Harold Liu
papers.summary: Vision language navigation (VLN) is very challenging for Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) since small errors in 3D motion prediction can lead to navigation errors and collisions. Unable to fathom execution outcomes in 3D environments, existing methods often struggle to predict accurate navigation waypoints from language instructions. To solve this, we introduce the Prototypical Visual Imagination framework, shortened as ProtoVis-Nav, which forces the model to imagine an outcome-associated local visual representation for the intended next UAV movement. Specifically, we predict feature prototypes and use their linear combination to estimate the visual feature of the target region. In this manner, the VLN model first imagines the local visual representation of the next intended location, and then uses predicted prototypes as context for generating the final action, promoting alignment between visual context and waypoint outputs. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the ProtoVis-Nav framework and show substantial improvements over existing baselines.

papers.title: Internalizing Investment Mandates: A Neurosymbolic RL Approach to Portfolio Allocation
papers.authors: Zeynep Yıldız, Satchit Chatterji, Ercan Atam, Erman Acar
papers.summary: Institutional portfolios operate under investment policy statements that specify asset allocation constraints, often conditioned on market regime information. Deep reinforcement learning has been shown to optimize financial performance but typically does not enforce rule compliance, making it unsuitable for real-world deployment. Existing neurosymbolic methods such as Probabilistic Logic Policy Gradient (PLPG) offer constraint-satisfying reinforcement learning (RL) via differentiable symbolic supervision but assume a finite, discrete action space. We present a PLPG-inspired continuous allocation method that estimates the probability that the policy's own executed action satisfies the investment mandate, using reparameterized Monte Carlo sampling, and adds it to the training objective. No post-hoc enforcement mechanism intercepts actions at inference time and compliance is learned by the agent. Audited directly on deterministic mean actions with no correction, the policy reduces violations of a six-rule regime-conditional mandate from 96-98% for unconstrained RL and 33.4% for a reward-penalty baseline to 4.8%, showing that a continuous-action neurosymbolic policy can substantially internalize a symbolic mandate.

papers.title: K2V: Generative Keyframing For Physically Plausible Video Generation
papers.authors: Felix O'Mahony, Daniel Olmeda Reino, Roberto Cipolla, Ayush Tewari
papers.summary: Video diffusion models are able to generate samples with high-quality appearance and textural qualities. However, content produced by these methods is known to exhibit significant physical errors. This is because, in a classical video generation setting, all physical reasoning must take place simultaneously and exclusively within the diffusion process.We propose to resolve these issues by redistributing the task of physical reasoning onto a language model-backed keyframe generation module, which allows for explicit reasoning in language, and fine-grained control over the appearance of the video at important moments in the video. We then condition a video generation model with these keyframes, reducing the role of the diffusion model to the simpler task of interpolating between physically-correct intermediate states, rather than inferring an entire sequence with diffusion. Results demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms existing approaches, achieving state-of-the-art performance on the Physics-IQ Verified benchmark and PhyGenBench.

papers.title: BrickFlow: Connectivity-Guided Brick Reconstruction
papers.authors: Peter Kulits, Cordelia Schmid
papers.summary: Given a set of LEGO parts and an image of an assembled object, our task is to infer the pose of each part to assemble the object. In contrast with traditional 3D reconstruction, doing so requires satisfying discrete physical constraints, which provide structure but render the problem combinatorial and highly sensitive to small pose errors. To learn a prior over how parts fit together, we train a set-conditioned SE(3) flow model on procedurally generated assemblies. We then finetune this model to inject image conditioning, using 1% as much data. However, while the learned flow captures global structure, it does not enforce connectivity. To address this, we introduce an analytic connectivity-field guidance to pull predictions toward connected assemblies at test time. Through this, we demonstrate improved build quality with model size, pretraining, and guidance. We make our models and data available for research purposes at https://kulits.github.io/BrickFlow/

papers.title: Where LLM Agents Get Stuck Debugging Databases: Access More Than Reasoning
papers.authors: Gustavo Pinto
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) coding agents are increasingly asked not only to write code but to debug running systems from live runtime data. We report a field observation of one such agent (Claude Code) as it diagnosed eight database incidents in a production message-dispatch engine. In every incident whose root cause depended on runtime concurrency, the agent announced a cause, shipped a fix, and later walked it back, and each wrong guess cost a deploy-and-observe cycle. Mapping each incident to what the agent lacked, we find that access to production state was the most pervasive bottleneck. The missing access included live lock views, untruncated deadlock reports, read-only execution, and an explicit environment context. An access gap was present in all five concurrency-dependent incidents: alone in one, and in four combined with a reasoning error such as anchoring on an early cause, incomplete exploration of the configuration, or a misreading of the code's transaction semantics. The three incidents that did not depend on concurrency needed nothing beyond what the agent already had. Within the incidents, the agent's wrong hypotheses were consistent with the evidence it could see; they were not fabrications. We argue that the next step for production-debugging agents is a forensics layer that gives the agent the access it lacks inside existing security controls. Such a layer would combine a safe interrogation API, a lock-and-deadlock flight recorder, and a production replay harness.

papers.title: Consistent Video-to-Video Translation via Explicit Correspondences
papers.authors: Gaurav Parmar, Zhengqi Li, Richard Zhang, Jun-Yan Zhu et al.
papers.summary: Interactive video-to-video applications require real-time generation while maintaining long-range temporal consistency. However, recent methods achieve speed by restricting attention to a fixed-length causal window. This limits long-range consistency whenever relevant history falls outside the context window. To address this limitation, we introduce vid2vid-long, a correspondence-based approach grounded in a simple observation. Video-to-video translation provides an explicit cross-frame reference: the regions that match in the input video should match in the output video too. Concretely, we compute patch-level correspondences in the input, guiding retrieval of previously generated outputs in the corresponding regions, and condition the model on these patches through correspondence cross-attention. Our experiments demonstrate that vid2vid-long consistently improves long-range temporal consistency across recent video models while preserving generation quality and real-time performance.

papers.title: Augmented Hybrid TV Services. Habits, Preferences, Opinions and Expectations of Spanish Consumers
papers.authors: Fernando Boronat, Bernat Roig, Enric Sigalat, Santiago J. Flores
papers.summary: The convergence of hybrid broadcast and broadband delivery, companion devices, and immersive technologies enables new forms of interactive, personalized, and accessible TV services. This paper introduces the concept of Augmented Hybrid TV services and presents an exploratory user requirements and preliminary acceptance assessment for 5 representative use cases. They were selected through an exploratory stakeholder consultation and 3 co-design workshops with audiovisual professionals and participants from organizations supporting people with visual or hearing impairments. They combine conventional TV with complementary content delivered to connected devices, including AR/VR HMD. They were subsequently evaluated through a cross-sectional CAWI survey of 626 Internet and connected TV users in Spain. Each participant viewed standardized video demonstrations of 2 randomly assigned cases and assessed their perceived usefulness, anticipated benefits/limitations, and interest in them. The results show substantial interest across all five use cases, ranging from 64.7% to 76.9%. Adaptive and personalized augmented subtitles received the highest level of interest and were particularly valued for their accessibility, language-learning, and personalization benefits. Immersive services involving complementary AR content, virtual screens, 3D objects, and 360 video were also evaluated positively, although participants identified device cost, ergonomics, connectivity, usability, and synchronization as anticipated limitations. The findings provide user-centered evidence that can inform the prioritization, design, and subsequent prototype-based evaluation of standards-compliant Augmented Hybrid TV services. Because the study assessed video-based scenarios rather than functional systems, the results represent perceived usefulness and stated interest rather than observed adoption or technically validated QoE.

papers.title: Patterns for Designing CI/CD Workflows
papers.authors: Leandro Sousa, Filipe Correia
papers.summary: CI/CD pipelines are difficult to build and maintain, and information about them is scattered across empirical studies, practitioner books, and catalogues of 'smells'. We collected candidate practices and anti-practices converted them into patterns, and then consolidated these into patterns. These patterns address issues such as security, pipeline scheduling, workflow structure, performance and failure and release management. Each pattern is contextualised and describes the problem it solves, the forces at play, the solution and the consequences.

papers.title: HEIR: Harness Egocentric Intent for Human-Robot Interactions
papers.authors: Yichi Zhang, Bo Wang, Zhenghan Zhu, Yutong Han et al.
papers.summary: For robots to assist, serve, and collaborate with humans, they must not only interpret human requests conveyed through language and multimodal intentional cues, but also execute long-horizon tasks that interleave navigation and manipulation. In this paper, we introduce HEIR, a resource for studying how to Harness Egocentric Intent for Human-Robot Interaction. HEIR pairs human speech, measured gaze, and egocentric video with robot observations and teleoperated navigation-manipulation trajectories, while each session preserves successive episodes, with each request fulfilled through multiple execution subtasks. The captured data, together with human-authored annotations, support the study of intent grounding, execution planning, and task completion within a unified interaction setting. To demonstrate the value of HEIR, we conduct extensive offline experiments to evaluate how models benefit from additional human-centric context across these tasks, together with real-robot experiments that assess execution task completion. HEIR thus provides a valuable resource for studying user-centric robot interaction in naturalistic household environments. Our demo and dataset are available online.

papers.title: Collaborative Task Allocation for Heterogeneous Multi-Robot Systems Through Iterative Clustering
papers.authors: David R. Martin, Brooks A. Butler, Scott Nivison, Magnus Egerstedt et al.
papers.summary: Multi-robot systems face the challenge of efficiently allocating teams of heterogeneous robots to tasks. The task allocation problem is complicated by collaborative interactions between robots where teams of robots develop emergent capabilities that enable them to complete tasks that would be inefficient or impossible for individual robots. To address these challenges, we present an iterative clustering algorithm for collaborative task allocation in heterogeneous multi-robot systems. This approach partitions the computationally intractable global optimization problem into smaller, tractable subproblems by iteratively forming clusters of robots and tasks, then optimizing assignments within each cluster. By ensuring robots remain clustered with their currently assigned tasks, we guarantee monotonic improvement in overall utility with each iteration. We analyze the convergence of the algorithm and characterize how cluster size constraints determine which suboptimal assignments could trap the algorithm. In simulation, iterative clustering consistently outperforms simulated annealing, and a group-based auction in both computation time and solution quality, and outperforms a hedonic game approach in solution quality.

papers.title: PACER: GPU Excursion Management for ML Workloads
papers.authors: Rutwik Jain, Nathaniel Morris, Yiwei Jiang, Shidhartha Das et al.
papers.summary: Variability is an inherent characteristic of modern GPU systems, arising from a combination of process variation, dynamic environmental conditions, and power management decisions. Prior work has characterized inter-GPU variability and found consistent performance differences across GPUs. However, we observe that modern workloads, particularly large language models (LLMs), exhibit significant intra-GPU variability. Their short-running kernels interact poorly with the coarse granularity of dynamic power management mechanisms, leading to unpredictable performance. A key source of this intra-GPU transient variability is power excursions, also referred to as electrical design power peaks (EDPp), where power temporarily exceeds the GPU's rated power limits. While power management mechanisms are designed to ensure reliable operation despite the presence of EDPp sustained power peaks cause throttling that detrimentally impacts overall application performance. To the best of our knowledge, our work is the first to characterize the magnitude and frequency of EDPp, showing that frequent, significant power overshoots are especially common in ML workloads, which combine high power draw, short kernels, and rapidly changing compute demands. To address this, we design and leverage hardware and firmware mechanisms to provide consistent power management behavior that reduces intra-GPU variability due to EDPp and improves overall performance. We evaluate our techniques across a range of popular workloads. Our approach improves performance by 3-12% over state-of-the-art GPU power management and comes within 3% of an oracular solution.

papers.title: Neural Render Proxies for Interactive and Differentiable Lighting
papers.authors: Sergio Sancho, Alexander Rath, Marco Manzi, Pascal Chang et al.
papers.summary: Within the CG animation production pipeline, the challenges artists tackle in Lighting can be immense. Even minor adjustments require re-rendering massive scenes with slow offline renderers; global illumination has to be sampled and complex shaders have to be evaluated, leading to iteration times of minutes to hours per frame. To accelerate this process, we introduce a novel neural render proxy (NRP) that enables differentiable relighting of static scenes with fixed camera and materials at interactive rates. Our main insight is the decoupling of traditional rendering into path sampling and emission computation. From a single, light-agnostic render pass, we collect light transport data in the form of path samples. This enables rapidly sampling lighting conditions on the fly, and training a scene-specific lightweight neural network that learns how light is transported from any scene location to any image pixel. This approach is compatible with non-differentiable production renderers, induces minimal memory requirements during inference, and scales only with resolution and the number of light sources and parameters, but independently of scene and appearance complexity. Our evaluation demonstrates interactive frame rates for relighting ( 30-60 Hz) while closely approximating the visual fidelity of ground-truth path tracing. In addition, the differentiable NRP enables fast, gradient-based inverse workflows, allowing artists to efficiently solve for lighting parameters from intuitive image-space edits or generative targets.

papers.title: Convolutional VocalTrax: Replacing Backpropagation Through Time with Convolution in Differentiable Articulatory Synthesis
papers.authors: Yongyi Zang, Debasish Ray Mohapatra, Randal Leistikow, Perry R. Cook
papers.summary: VocalTrax recovers interpretable articulatory controls from a recording by gradient descent through a differentiable Pink Trombone synthesizer. Its vocal tract is a Kelly-Lochbaum waveguide updated twice per audio sample, so every gradient step backpropagates through a long recurrence, which is slow on GPUs. We propose Convolutional VocalTrax, which computes the exact frequency response of the same waveguide and applies it as a causal convolution. We assume that the tract is stationary within 5.8 ms blocks and that its lossy impulse response can be truncated after 93 ms. Gradients then pass through FFTs and a short recursion along the tract instead of through time. On 600 AudioMNIST recordings, the tract forward and backward pass runs 47 to 63 times faster on an A100 GPU, and a classifier trained only on real speech recognizes our reconstructions more often than those of VocalTrax (14.5% vs. 10.0%), although the log-mel distance to the target is 11% higher. Parameters fitted with our model keep this gain when rendered by the original VocalTrax (13.8%).

papers.title: UAV-Flow++: A Unified Suite for Benchmarking and Learning Language-Guided UAV Flight
papers.authors: Donglin Yang, Xiangyu Wang, Yantong Zhong, Wenhao Zheng et al.
papers.summary: Language-guided UAV navigation has largely focused on long-horizon route planning, leaving short-range, object-relative flight maneuvers underexplored. To address this gap, we formulate Flying-on-a-Word (Flow), a task requiring a UAV to convert concise natural-language instruction, egocentric visual observation, and current state dynamics into continuous flight actions. Flow encompasses both primitive motion commands and complex object-interactive behaviors, assessing motion intent comprehension and spatial context grounding. To enable policy learning and closed-loop evaluation, we introduce UAV-Flow, a comprehensive dataset comprising 30,692 expert-piloted real-world trajectories across eight distinct motion categories, alongside 10,109 simulation trajectories in the UAV-Flow-Sim environment equipped with task-specific completion criteria. Furthermore, we develop FlowVLA, which undergoes imitation pretraining on mixed real-sim demonstrations and online post-training via Tail-Aware GRPO (TGRPO). By leveraging group reward distributions, TGRPO effectively reinforces high-reward action sequences. Evaluated on 273 held-out UAV-Flow-Sim episodes, pretrained FlowVLA achieves a mean success rate of 75.58%, outperforming the strongest baseline by 6.72 percentage points, which TGRPO post-training further elevates to 93.16% with superior sample efficiency. Physical UAV experiments demonstrate robust execution of object-relative commands in both indoor and outdoor real-world scenes. Together, Flow establishes a novel benchmark and learning framework for language-conditioned flight maneuvers.

papers.title: XBot-Omni: An Omni-Modal Model for Embodied Understanding and Interaction
papers.authors: Kerui Gu, Xing Fu, Shuoyang Sun, Cheng Peng et al.
papers.summary: Embodied interaction requires an agent to integrate multimodal perception with verbal and nonverbal behaviors to effectively communicate its intentions, including speech, body motion, and facial expressions. We present XBot-Omni, a Thinker–Talker–Actor architecture that extends the Omni paradigm to robotic modalities, including body motion and facial expressions, with ``X'' representing the extensibility to robotic-specific modalities. The Thinker processes text, images, audio, and video to formulate contextually appropriate responses, which are then realized by the Talker and Actor through speech and coordinated bodily expressions, respectively. In this report, we innovatively introduce the concept of ``Actor'' as a dedicated component for embodied agents: a coordinated, streaming module that leverages the native representations of the Thinker and Talker within an end-to-end pipeline, introducing only modest latency overhead. This unified architecture enables multimodal generation conditioned on omni-modal inputs directly to prevent information loss in staged designs. We comprehensively evaluate XBot-Omni across seven benchmarks, demonstrating strong multimodal understanding capabilities on both general-domain and robot-centric videos, as well as high-quality, natural, and well-coordinated motion generation. Furthermore, our results validate its capability to generate embodied multimodal responses directly from omni inputs, meeting the diverse requirements of embodied interaction. XBot-Omni enables robots not only to perceive the omni world but also to express themselves through speech and bodily behaviors, extending Omni models from conversational interaction to embodied communication in physical environments.

papers.title: Inner Product Regularization for Imitation Learning
papers.authors: Benjamin A. Christie, Tianyu Qiu, Amy H. Choi, David Fridovich-Keil et al.
papers.summary: Robots that learn from demonstrations should extrapolate their policy despite state perturbations such as sensor noise, scene variation, and compounding errors. One approach to this robustness is regularization. Prior regularizers consider each state on its own and limit how sensitive the policy is to any perturbation at that state. By contrast, we explore how the policy's output shifts when given the same perturbation at different states. Our insight is that, locally, the robot should respond to state perturbations in a consistent manner: e.g., if changing an irrelevant object position does not impact the policy at one state, that same change should not shift the policy output at a nearby state. Applying this insight, we develop inner product regularization (InneR). We show that the inner product on action space induces an inner product on state space through the policy Jacobian (the Fisher information for stochastic policies), and that the null space of this inner product governs which state perturbations have a first-order effect on the policy. By clustering states whose inner products are aligned, averaging the inner products within each cluster, and minimizing the smallest eigenvalues of that average, InneR shapes the learned policy so that nearby states share a common null space. InneR enforces consistent responses to perturbations without limiting policy expressiveness, and can be appended to existing imitation learning pipelines for deterministic or stochastic policies. In simulated experiments, InneR makes learned policies more robust to irrelevant state dimensions and shifts between training and test distributions, whereas norm penalties often perform worse than behavior cloning. On a real robot arm performing three manipulation tasks, InneR raises the average success rate of a diffusion policy from 18% to 57% without additional data.

papers.title: Preserve the Vulnerability, Break the Alert: Testing the Robustness of CodeQL Taint Tracking with Natural Rewrites
papers.authors: Zhezhen Cao, Weiyuan Ding, Bowen Xu
papers.summary: Static application security testing (SAST) tools such as CodeQL serve as security gates in continuous integration and code review, and a gate is also read in reverse. When a previously reported alert disappears after a change, developers and the tools around them often take the vulnerability to be gone. That inference holds only if the analyzer is robust to changes that keep the vulnerability. We test this robustness for CodeQL's JavaScript taint tracking with natural, vulnerability-preserving rewrites. A large language model, given only the alert CodeQL exposes and no knowledge of its implementation, rewrites one function along a reported flow as a plausible maintenance change, and we verify by manual audit and controlled experiments that the flaw survives and the alert does not. On 172 flows that CodeQL detects in real npm vulnerabilities, three rewrites per flow silence 26.2% of them, at about USD 0.51 per silenced flow. The same generator, asked only to refactor the same functions with no knowledge of the alert, silences none of them. Every silencing rewrite traces to one of seven gaps at the library-modeling boundary, and 64 of the 70 rewrites cross a gap inside an API CodeQL already models. The largest is the WHATWG URL constructor, which propagates taint to a URL's query components but not to its pathname. The boundary is not specific to CodeQL. 74% of the silencing rewrites also silence an independently built taint analyzer, and 53% escape three analyzers combined. A disappearing alert after an ordinary-looking change is therefore weak evidence that a vulnerability has been fixed, the gaps point SAST developers to narrow and concrete repair targets, and robustness to natural rewrites belongs alongside detection rate in how taint analyzers are evaluated.

papers.title: On cryptographically non-linear all-or-nothing transforms
papers.authors: Anantajeet Devaraj, Navid Nasr Esfahani
papers.summary: An unconditionally secure (t, s, v)-all-or-nothing transform (AONT) is a bijection from s input elements to s output elements over an alphabet of size v, such that given any s - t output elements, no information can be obtained about any t input elements. While linear AONTs have been extensively studied, comparatively little is known about the existence of non-linear AONTs. In this paper, we investigate unconditionally secure cryptographically non-linear (t, s, v)-AONTs, distinguishing between non-additivity, non-affinity, and cryptographic non-linearity. To achieve this, we first present a computational method for enumerating general AONTs focusing on the case (t, 3, 3)-AONTs for t = 1 and 2, establishing the existence of non-additive AONTs. We then introduce a general construction of non-additive AONTs from linear ones using coordinate-wise symbol permutations. We measure the non-linearity of the AONT instances generated from this construction, using differential ΔF-uniformity and Walsh magnitude. Finally, we establish theoretical conditions under which ΔF-uniformity is reduced and present statistical results examining the non-linearity of AONTs obtained through our construction.

papers.title: A Compact xDAWN-Guided Spatio-Temporal Network with Filter-Bank Convolution for P300 Detection
papers.authors: Mohammad Mahdi Habibi Bina, Mohammad Reza Daliri
papers.summary: P300-based brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) enable communication by decoding stimulus-evoked EEG responses into character selections without requiring voluntary motor output. Reliable P300 detection remains difficult because of low response amplitude and signal-to-noise ratio, while practical spellers require accurate character selection with few stimulus repetitions and low computational cost. We propose a compact deep learning architecture that combines xDAWN spatial filtering for event-related potential enhancement and dimensionality reduction, a fixed frequency-selective filter bank, and convolutional feature learning for spatio-temporal EEG decoding. Depthwise-separable convolutions and progressive average pooling reduce computational complexity while retaining discriminative temporal information. The resulting target/non-target classifier contains only 5,100 trainable parameters. We evaluated the model on two public benchmarks, BCI Competition II Dataset IIb and BCI Competition III Dataset II, and compared it with established P300 decoding methods across different numbers of stimulus repetitions. The model achieved an information transfer rate of 17.8 bits/min with two repetitions on BCI Competition III and 40.5 bits/min on BCI Competition II, demonstrating a favorable accuracy-speed trade-off. These results suggest that combining domain-informed spatial and spectral priors with compact neural networks can support efficient P300 decoding for EEG-based BCI communication.

papers.title: NonSense: On the (In)security of FPGA Anti-tamper Sensors
papers.authors: Mehmet Ali Cetin, Fatemeh Khojasteh Dana, Saleh Khalaj Monfared, Nima Seyed Aghazadeh et al.
papers.summary: FPGAs are widely used in mission-critical systems, where a successful physical attack can have serious consequences. This makes resilience to such attacks a critical security requirement. To defend against active physical attacks, such as glitching attacks, modern FPGAs rely on on-chip sensors that detect these disturbances and trigger responses, such as key zeroization, before a device is compromised. These sensors are deployed as both hard-IP blocks and soft-IP cores, and their trustworthiness is often taken for granted. In this work, we challenge that assumption and argue that the sensors themselves are a fragile and underexplored attack surface. Drawing on recent results, we show that both the detection and response mechanisms of state-of-the-art sensors can be bypassed without invasive tampering. We further argue that sensor reliability is reduced by factors rarely captured in threat models, including the spatial and frequency-dependent behavior of the system's power delivery network, which can steer a fault to a target while sparing nearby sensors; environmental conditions such as temperature, which shift detection thresholds; and long-term aging, which drifts sensor calibration and may open silent detection gaps. Finally, we propose a set of countermeasures that harden detection and response mechanisms against these effects.

papers.title: Neural Representations as New Modes of Interactivity
papers.authors: Stanley Huang, Anthony Baez, Catherine Yeh, Pat Pataranutaporn
papers.summary: Human-AI interaction today runs almost entirely through prompts and outputs, keeping AI systems opaque to general users. We introduce Neural Representation Interaction (NRI), a paradigm that treats the internal representations of neural networks as an interaction material people can inspect, steer, and edit. Situating NRI alongside graphical, tangible, and bio-computer interaction, we argue that the concepts and algorithms models encode internally offer representational affordances for richer human-AI interaction. We synthesize actionable mechanistic interpretability methods and, drawing on General Morphological Analysis, construct a design space spanning Interaction, Target, Referent, and Purpose. Mapping existing interfaces onto this space reveals that most serve expert auditors, while few support lay users. We then present speculative applications in education, personal user modeling, and hiring audits, and discuss design principles, limitations, and sociotechnical risks. NRI offers HCI researchers abstractions for designing interactions that work with AI computation rather than only through its inputs and outputs.

papers.title: Exploring Socially Acceptable 3D Feedback Design for Inclusive Small-Group Conversation
papers.authors: Qianjie Wei, Yifan Li, Zhen Bai
papers.summary: Prior research has shown that providing feedback on group dynamics can improve the quality of small-group conversations. However, publicly delivered feedback that targets specific individuals may reduce social acceptability due to negative experiences such as social pressure, embarrassment, and resistance. This work investigates how public feedback can be designed to remain socially acceptable while maintaining its effectiveness in XR-based small-group conversations. Informed by social science and HCI literature, we identified three design strategies (incorporate humor, reduce social attention, and use indirectness) and proposed a set of metaphor- and agent-based 3D feedback probes. We then conducted a two-phase study: (1) an online survey with 50 participants to examine how such feedback designs are perceived under public and private delivery, and (2) follow-up interviews with 14 participants who completed the survey to better understand their interpretations and elicit additional insights. Results show that metaphor- and agent-based feedback can reduce social discomfort while maintaining effectiveness. Interview findings further highlighted the role of three strategies in making feedback easier to accept, while requiring careful balance. We also discussed design implications for creating socially acceptable 3D feedback to support inclusive small-group conversations in XR.

papers.title: DiffSSMEye: Conditional High-Frequency Eye Movement Synthesis with Structured State-Space Diffusion
papers.authors: Kamrul Hasan, Mehedi Hasan Raju, Oleg V. Komogortsev
papers.summary: Synthesizing high-frequency eye movements requires preserving long-range temporal dependencies and subject-specific oculomotor dynamics. However, methods based on generative adversarial networks (GANs) and variational autoencoders (VAEs) can struggle to preserve these characteristics simultaneously. We introduce DiffSSMEye, a conditional denoising diffusion probabilistic model with bidirectional Structured State Space Sequence (S4) layers for generating five-second gaze-velocity sequences at 1,000 Hz. Generation is conditioned on a coarse gaze reference, user identity, and task, where identity and task embeddings are incorporated through feature-wise linear modulation. Identity-preservation, multi-resolution spectral, and integrated-drift losses complement noise prediction to constrain biometric consistency, frequency structure, and displacement error. Subject-disjoint evaluation on GazeBase across seven tasks yields mean real–synthetic embedding cosine similarities of 0.91–0.95. DiffSSMEye also achieves the lowest median spatial errors among these baselines for horizontal and random saccade tasks. These results demonstrate improved spatial accuracy and biometric feature consistency for subject-specific gaze synthesis.

papers.title: Anonymous in Name Only: A Critical Review and a Reidentification Exercise on the European Commission's Anonymization Measures for Google Search Data under Article 6(11) of the DMA
papers.authors: David Sánchez, Benet Manzanares, Josep Domingo-Ferrer
papers.summary: In July 2026, the European Commission (EC) set out the anonymization measures Alphabet must implement to share Google Search data with competing search engines under Article 6(11) of the Digital Markets Act. As the first concrete illustration of how the EC operationalizes anonymization under the EU digital rulebook, this methodology could become a regulatory benchmark. In this paper, we show why it should not. We critically review the anonymization measures proposed by the EC, from the characterization of residual risk to the suppression thresholds and the reliance on contractual safeguards. For each of those issues, we highlight significant conceptual flaws, and, where applicable, we illustrate these flaws with empirical observations from real Google Search data provided by Alphabet and protected under the EC's measures. Importantly, we present examples of low-effort reidentification, record linkage, and confidential attribute inference achieved through straightforward and automatable attack patterns. Our findings show that the approach of the EC relies on unjustified heuristics rather than formal privacy guarantees, underestimates the risks inherent in free-text search queries, and sacrifices data utility without achieving meaningful protection. We also demonstrate that the proposed measures do not meet any of the three anonymization criteria established by the European Data Protection Board (EDPB): no record isolation, no linkage, and no inference. Practitioners and regulators are therefore cautioned against treating these measures as a sound anonymization practice.

papers.title: Maturity²: Assessing the Maturity of Crypto Agility Maturity Models
papers.authors: Leonie Wolf, Robin Leander Schröder, Sebastian Schinzel, Fabian Ising
papers.summary: Crypto agility maturity models aim to support organizations in preparing for cryptographic transitions, such as migrating to post-quantum cryptography. Recognizing the importance of measurable maturity, NIST references several such models in its guidance. Given NIST's influence on cybersecurity practice, these models may shape organizational planning and governance mechanisms. However, their design quality has not been systematically evaluated. In this work, we assess three industry-driven maturity models against established design principles. Our analysis reveals recurring weaknesses, particularly the lack of measurable, reproducible assessment criteria and limited prescriptive guidance for improving crypto agility. At the same time, we highlight individual strengths that can assist practitioners in choosing among the models and derive concrete recommendations for strengthening future crypto agility maturity models.

papers.title: It Was Better Not to Know: Digital Recognition, Family Authority, and Postpartum Mental Health in Bangladesh
papers.authors: Shajnin Haque Aishy, Sabbir Bin Abdul Latif, Md. Golam Zel A Husna, Jannatun Noor
papers.summary: Postpartum mental distress affects roughly one in five mothers in low- and lower-middle-income countries, yet recognition and support remain limited where formal mental-health care is scarce, and family relationships govern health decisions. We report a five-month interview study with 20 mothers in urban, urban slum, and rural Bangladesh who had given birth within the previous two years. Mothers encountered the concept of postpartum depression incidentally, through Facebook and YouTube recommendations rather than deliberate search or clinical guidance, and then used these platforms for private sensemaking without disclosing. Recognition, however, rarely traveled beyond the self: mothers could identify their distress while families dismissed it, leaving them with knowledge but no authority to act. Participants sought validation as a precondition for support and described recovery as relational rather than clinical or digital. We argue that postpartum technologies should engage partners, families, and community health workers rather than placing recognition solely on mothers.

papers.title: Kezek: Splitting Mono Two-Person Conversations into Per-Speaker Tracks for Full-Duplex Dialogue Data
papers.authors: Bagzhan Karl, Alizhan Karl
papers.summary: Full-duplex spoken dialogue models learn turn-taking, overlaps and backchannels from conversations recorded with one channel per speaker, but most available conversational audio is a single mono mix. We present Kezek, a model that turns a mono recording of exactly two people into one track per person with the original length and timing; overlaps and short replies ("yeah", "mm-hm") stay on the track of the person who said them. Kezek decides who speaks when and who is who once for the whole recording (stage 1: a two-voice activity model guided by a speaker fingerprint trained to be insensitive to phase), and a conditioned time-domain separator only carries out that decision (stage 2), with outputs that always sum to the input. Standard separation metrics miss the failures that matter for dialogue data, so we report short-reply retention, leakage onto the other person's solo, channel swaps and coverage. Against the open pipeline pyannote -> DialogueSidon on the same recordings, Kezek keeps more short replies (0.83 vs. 0.69 on Open Yap test; 0.80 vs. 0.71 over the other's speech on unseen telephone speech from CallHome English), mostly because it returns the whole recording while the external pipeline drops part of it (on the audio both return, reply retention is about the same: 0.859 vs. 0.865 on Open Yap); it also leaks less, swaps channels less often, and runs 4-5 times faster (about 230 hours of audio per GPU-hour). We also report negative results and an ideal-mask ceiling that locate the remaining gap: quiet replies under a louder voice. Code and weights are released under permissive licences.

papers.title: STEALTH: Steganographic Text Encoding Agnostic to Low-Level Tensor Hardware
papers.authors: William Fleshman
papers.summary: Provably secure linguistic steganography hides a message inside text sampled from a language model, so that without the key, a stegotext is computationally indistinguishable from an honest model sample. Nearly every such scheme assumes the receiver can recompute the sender's token probabilities exactly bit for bit. We show this assumption is fragile: across three model families, bit-exact schemes decode almost none of our messages once the receiver's floating-point precision, quantization, or GPU architecture differs from the sender's, or even when the receiver merely scores a text in parallel versus one token at a time, with the same model, precision, and hardware held fixed. We present STEALTH, a scheme built for exactly this setting. The sender draws each token with an exponential race driven by keyed pseudorandom noise, so a receiver's probability mismatch flips a token only when the race is close; a rateless spinal code, decoded by beam search, absorbs the resulting flips without the sender and receiver ever agreeing on a single distribution. We prove stegotexts remain indistinguishable from honest samples under this construction. Empirically, STEALTH decodes every message we sent for every receiver in the sender's model family, at every precision and quantization level, on smaller models, and on a different GPU architecture. STEALTH is even robust across different model families with separate vocabularies and tokenizers, decoding every message we tested. Our approach carries far more payload per token than prior robust schemes, and trained steganalyzers and a targeted statistical test both fail to distinguish its stegotexts from honest model output.

papers.title: Non-Functional Requirements to Hyperparameter Translation for Quantum Software via LLMs
papers.authors: Joseph G. Bronyah, Nasir U. Eisty
papers.summary: Quantum software engineering (QSE) lacks validated approaches for translating natural-language non-functional requirements (NFRs) into execution parameters such as shots and transpiler optimization levels. Existing methods emphasize semantic similarity rather than execution outcomes. We evaluate seven large language models (LLMs) against a deterministic heuristic baseline using 540 synthetic and 18 real-world user stories. We assess semantic accuracy and execution outcomes, including time, cost, top-state probability, and two-qubit gate exposure, through Qiskit/Aer simulations. All LLMs significantly outperformed the heuristic in semantic accuracy, achieving 55.6 to 83.3 percent on real-world stories compared to 16.7 percent for the heuristic. However, no LLM demonstrated statistically significant superiority over others on the real-world dataset. Speed- and cost-oriented configurations reduced execution time and cost, but fidelity improvements were not supported. Some failures resulted from provider safety refusals rather than translation errors. Our findings demonstrate the potential of LLMs as middleware for NFR-to-configuration translation in QSE, while emphasizing execution-based validation, human oversight, and careful interpretation of model differences.

papers.title: Collision-Resilient All-to-All Broadcast Scheduling in Underwater Acoustic Networks
papers.authors: Guoliang Weng, Enqi Zhang, Lizhao You, Deqing Wang et al.
papers.summary: This paper studies all-to-all broadcast scheduling for underwater swarms with collision-resilient physical layers that can decode asynchronously overlapping packets. Propagation-aware collision-free schedulers coordinate packet arrivals but do not account for this reception capability. We first design a data-driven neural reception model that captures per-interferer power and timing effects. The model improves prediction accuracy over SINR baselines while admitting an exact mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) formulation. The resulting neural-network-embedded MILP (NN-MILP) optimizes transmission times while explicitly encoding schedule-dependent overlaps and the predictor's inference, enabling globally optimal scheduling for small-scale instances. For larger networks, a two-stage ant colony optimization (ACO) heuristic combines low-cost transmission-order search with neural-aware timing refinement. Simulation results show that ACO shortens broadcast rounds compared with existing schedulers. It approaches the NN-MILP optimum on small-scale instances while supporting larger networks at substantially lower computational cost.

papers.title: Context Graph: Explainable Multi-Agent Decision Chains in AI-RAN
papers.authors: Xijun Wang, Zhaoyang Liu, Xiang Chen, Howard H. Yang et al.
papers.summary: AI-RAN distributes network control across multiple autonomous agents, namely xApps and rApps operating over shared radio resources. When an alert or degradation appears, operators currently lack a structured way to trace which decision caused it, what context triggered that decision, and how other agents interacted. Existing explainability tools focus on single-model feature attribution or linear event logging, neither of which captures cross-agent decision chains. We propose the Context Graph, a heterogeneous directed graph that organizes policies, measurements, decisions, and alerts into a queryable explanation layer. Its foundational primitive is the Decision-Event node acting as a causal junction, where incoming edges capture triggering context and outgoing edges track downstream consequences that are progressively upgraded through counterfactual verification. Instantiated over existing E2, A1, and O1 data flows, our proof-of-concept demonstrates that compliance and diagnosis queries are resolved at sub-millisecond latency over graphs of tens of thousands of nodes, while reliably distinguishing true causal impacts from spurious correlations.

papers.title: Topology-Aware Handover Management for Service Continuity in LEO Satellite Networks
papers.authors: Jui-Che Han, Nasir Khan, Siva Satya Sri Ganesh Seeram, Cicek Cavdar
papers.summary: Low Earth orbit (LEO) satellites are expected to play a key role in sixth-generation (6G) non-terrestrial networks. The high mobility of LEO satellites necessitates frequent handovers (HOs), posing challenges to service continuity and availability for user equipment. Conventional methods based on handover margin (HOM) and time-to-trigger (TTT) have limited adaptability to time-varying channel conditions and do not explicitly account for the impact of feeder-link and ground station (GS) connectivity on HO interruption time. To address these limitations, this paper develops a topology-aware HO framework based on proximal policy optimization (PPO). The framework uses reference signal received power (RSRP), satellite–GS associations, remaining visibility time, and elevation angles to determine when to initiate an HO and which satellite to select. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed policy achieves a service availability of 99.32% at a minimum elevation angle of 40 degrees, exceeding that of optimized HOM–TTT (O-HT) and least-delay (LD) satellite selection by 1.67 and 1.41 percentage points, respectively. The policy maintains service availability above 97.52% as the minimum elevation angle increases to 55 degrees, demonstrating its ability to sustain high service availability under stricter elevation constraints.

papers.title: Locality Meets Interference: Structure and Scheduling in Radio Multicasting
papers.authors: Qin Xin
papers.summary: We study multipoint-to-multipoint multicasting in synchronous radio networks with unknown participant locations and unrestricted message aggregation. Let n be the network size, k the number of participants, and d their hop diameter. A supplied distance-two coloring with C colors yields completion within (C-1)d+1 slots and at most nk transmissions. In unit disk graphs, coordinates, one-hop neighbor data, and a common degree bound Δ₀ suffice for a 15(Δ₀+1)-color schedule. A known fixed separation bound permits optimal deterministic Θ(d) completion from coordinates alone. Without geometric data, strong selectivity gives O(dn,(Δ₀+1)² n) slots when n is known. Independent random transmission gives O((Δ₀+1)(d+(k/η))) slots with failure probability at most η; for fixed Δ₀, this simplifies to O(d+(1/η)). A star construction shows that the logarithmic term is necessary for this random rule when the degree grows. We extend color schedules to fixed deletions and subgraphs connected over bounded windows of cycles. Separate conditional reductions preserve additive costs under diameter guessing and control parameter-table and cluster preprocessing. Finally, a counterexample shows that pruning and reranking a breadth-first tree can destroy interference-free delivery. For one-hop designated delivery with receiver degree at most b, we prove that the optimal schedule length equals the chromatic number of an associated conflict graph and is at most 2b-1, with matching examples.

papers.title: Agentic Orchestration for SLA-Constrained Network Slicing in Programmable Mobile Data Planes
papers.authors: Rodrigo Moreira, Larissa Ferreira Rodrigues Moreira, Joberto S. B. Martins, Tereza C. Carvalho et al.
papers.summary: The Third Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) Technical Specification 23.501 (Release 17) defines Maximum Bit Rate (MBR) enforcement at the User Plane Function (UPF) in fifth-generation (5G) networks. Supporting differentiated service-level agreements across the radio access and core networks requires the UPF to enforce MBR limits according to configured slice priorities. During overload, the challenge is to adapt these limits while preserving that differentiation and avoiding oscillations. Building on programmable enforcement and intelligent orchestration, we propose an agentic control loop combining UPF telemetry with locally hosted Large Language Model (LLM) selection from a finite set of admissible rate candidates. Deterministic logic validates each selection and derives Packet Forwarding Control Protocol (PFCP) updates. The evaluated runs show no oscillations or fallbacks and unchanged highest-priority rate limits. These observations establish configuration preservation; delivered per-class QoS protection remains unmeasured.

papers.title: MESH: Multi-receiver Evaluation of Spatial Hearing across Egocentric and Allocentric Views
papers.authors: Wen Wen, Bohan Li, KwanHo Tam, Yu Xi et al.
papers.summary: Spatial hearing in multi-receiver environments requires identifying who speaks, where they are, and how they move. Existing benchmarks evaluate spatial prediction, transcription, tracking, and distributed speech processing, but offer limited evaluation of whether speech signal remains associated with the correct physical source across receivers and motion. We introduce MESH, which evaluates this association through egocentric and allocentric views of shared acoustic scenes. The egocentric view uses local recordings and peer metadata, while the allocentric view combines synchronized recordings from multiple receivers in a shared 3D world frame. MESH contains nearly 40,000 questions across 13 static and dynamic localization and spatial transcription tasks. We evaluate eleven audio-model configurations and a language-model agent using specialist tools. The best static distance-estimation and dynamic direction-tracking accuracies are only 21.90% and 41.54%, respectively, while the lowest word error rates across four transcription tasks range from 59.15% to 73.10%. Ablation studies and additional experiments reveal that existing models are not yet able to effectively leverage peer information and struggle to handle multi-speaker and dynamic scenarios. These findings highlight the gap between access to distributed acoustic information and its effective use for spatial speech understanding. We release the dataset and evaluation code to support further research on collaborative and distributed spatial hearing.

papers.title: MusicRWKV: A Multimodal RWKV Framework for Music Representation Learning
papers.authors: Terry Tan
papers.summary: Recent music foundation models have achieved remarkable progress in music representation learning, yet most existing approaches rely on Transformer architectures whose quadratic attention complexity introduces substantial computational and memory overhead when modeling long-duration music recordings. In this work, we propose MusicRWKV, a multimodal music representation learning framework built upon the RWKV architecture. MusicRWKV jointly models waveform, spectrogram, and metadata information within a unified self-supervised learning framework. To improve efficiency for long musical sequences, we introduce an invertible compression module that reduces sequence length while preserving reconstruction capability. A FiLM-based conditioning strategy is employed to facilitate modality-aware representation learning without introducing expensive cross-attention operations. We further investigate the integration of Soft ROSA as a differentiable retrieval mechanism for neural-symbolic interaction. Experimental evaluation across a diverse collection of Music Information Retrieval (MIR) benchmarks demonstrates that the proposed RWKV-based architecture can be effectively adapted to heterogeneous music understanding tasks. A controlled pretraining ablation shows that Soft ROSA improves validation performance, while layer-wise telemetry analysis reveals a progressive transition from distributed retrieval to selective retrieval in deeper network layers. These results suggest that RWKV provides a promising architectural alternative to Transformer-based models for multimodal music understanding.

papers.title: Sprint3D: Accelerating End-to-End 3D Asset Generation through Pipeline Optimization
papers.authors: Sho Kuno, Ruihan Yu, Yonghao Yu, Guixu Lin et al.
papers.summary: Image-to-3D generative models now produce asset-quality textured meshes, but at minutes per asset they remain slow to iterate with and costly to deploy. Prior work has mostly accelerated the sampling of the networks, and where it also optimizes the mesh processing, it trains its own generators. We instead start from a publicly released pipeline and ask how much of its end-to-end time can be saved. Profiling the public Pixal3D pipeline shows that its latency is dominated by what happens after the networks: the four rectified flows take 14% of the wall-clock time and mesh post-processing takes 85%, most of it in CPU-based UV unwrapping. We therefore first rebuild the mesh post-processing on the GPU and take it off the critical path, then cut the per-evaluation overhead of the flows and distill them from 76 to 8 network evaluations. The resulting pipeline, Sprint3D, reduces the median time per asset from 133 s to 4.05 s on one H200 GPU at the same export settings (33×). At the same time, on 2,653 held-out Toys4K objects it improves every input-view normal metric of the Pixal3D protocol, with a slightly lower mean silhouette IoU, lower point-cloud alignment scores and less fine texture detail. The rebuilt post-processing alone also speeds up TRELLIS.2, which uses the same export code, by 6.7× without a detectable change in the evaluated metrics.

papers.title: PIM: A Physical Intuition Model for Low-Latency Prediction of Object Interaction Outcomes
papers.authors: Tangwen Luo, Chuankun Zheng, Yuchi Huo
papers.summary: Predicting object interaction outcomes from initial conditions is a central problem in data-driven physical reasoning. Existing methods often use rigid-body-level states or predict the evolution through autoregressive rollouts. Coarse representations cannot represent local deformation, while rollout errors may compound over long prediction horizons. Instead, we introduce PIM, a Physical Intuition Model that directly predicts a physical system's equilibrium state from its initial mesh geometry, kinematics, and physical attributes. PIM combines local k-nearest-neighbor (KNN) attention to encode intra-object geometry, anchor-based cross-object attention to model interactions, and a dual-branch decoder that predicts object-level translations and per-vertex residual displacements. Across MuJoCo scenarios involving both rigid and deformable interactions, PIM achieves lower vertex and centroid errors than the evaluated baselines. By predicting complete equilibrium states in a single forward pass, PIM substantially reduces latency relative to autoregressive learned models and MuJoCo rollouts under the evaluated protocols, enabling low-latency inference when only the final outcome is required.

papers.title: People prefer AI to human advice in multi-turn conversations but neither changes incentivised behaviour
papers.authors: Maximilian Maier, Tsz Kwan Emmy Wong, Jiahao Eric Yang, Falk Lieder et al.
papers.summary: People increasingly ask AI chatbots for advice, yet large language models (LLMs) are sycophantic, overconfident, and can amplify human cognitive biases. In this article, we investigate how people perceive advice from humans versus LLMs and whether AI advice reshapes incentive-compatible donation decisions. Using Carrier, a new experimental platform, we designed an experiment where participants made a donation decision after discussing it with an AI chatbot advisor, another human, or receiving no advice. Participants judged LLM advisors to be significantly more rational, trustworthy, convincing, and sycophantic than human advisors. Analysis of chatlogs showed that LLMs were more engaged than human advisors: they shared more facts and more often stated their opinion and justified their recommendations. Despite this, donation decisions did not vary across conditions.

papers.title: The Unseen Threat: How Complementary Combinations of Acoustic Features Compromise Speech Privacy
papers.authors: Jule Pohlhausen, Jörg Bitzer
papers.summary: The interaction of acoustic features in leaking private information remains underexplored. This work focuses on time-domain features, i.e., broadband RMS level and pitch, alone and combined with temporally smoothed and subsampled Mel spectrograms. Privacy is assessed using informed automatic speech recognition and speaker-verification attacks, while utility for conversational analysis is evaluated using voice activity detection and speaker diarisation. RMS level and pitch alone exposed limited information, but fusion with 500 ms-smoothed Mel spectrograms enhanced utility while substantially increasing speech-content leakage. Specifically, the combination with RMS level showed that fine-grained temporal dynamics can amplify leakage from coarsely sampled spectral features. Speaker-identity protection remained limited for all tested features. Overall, these findings indicate that privacy assessments performed on individual acoustic features may underestimate leakage after feature fusion.

papers.title: Rasoi: Visual Diffs for Evaluating Structural Changes Made by Coding Agents
papers.authors: Riya Sahni, Aryan Kaul, Anushka Bhatnagar, Xuanming Zhang et al.
papers.summary: Coding agents let developers modify software rapidly through natural language. However, as agents take on larger changes, developers can lose track of how the codebase is evolving. These edits may look correct on the surface while restructuring the system in unexpected ways: duplicating logic, changing modules outside the requested scope, removing functionality developers meant to keep, or introducing architectural drift. We investigate how visual diffs can help developers understand and evaluate the structural changes that coding agents make. We present Rasoi, a design probe that maps how a codebase's architecture evolves after each agent-made edit, letting developers inspect which architectural elements and relationships were added, modified, or removed across multiple levels of abstraction. We deployed Rasoi in a week-long study with 12 developers working on their own codebases across varied technical domains. We found that visual diffs helped developers see whether changes stayed within scope, notice unexpected restructuring, and understand how modified parts related to the system as a whole. Our findings suggest that the value of oversight tools for coding agents lies less in making developers trust the agent and more in helping developers feel confident in their own evaluation of agent-made changes. We discuss implications for visual tools that support code comprehension and human oversight in AI-assisted software development.

papers.title: Eliciting and Mitigating Specification Satisficing in Coding Agents
papers.authors: Ruixin Wang, Tianyi Zhang
papers.summary: Coding agents often fail to meet all requirements in the task description. In some of these failures, the agent considers an implementation choice that meets a requirement, but later decides to commit to another one that does not meet the requirement for a reason it finds acceptable. We call this specification satisficing. It is challenging to identify and mitigate specification satisficing because the agent accepts such choices for its own reasons, and existing self-correction methods are biased toward them. We propose SatisFix, which guides a coding agent to report these choices and their reasons, and then check each choice against the task description. We evaluate SatisFix on DeepSWE and SWE-bench Pro with five LLMs as backbones and two different agent frameworks, and compare it with three self-correction methods. SatisFix improves the pass@1 of the base agent by an average of 5.09% on DeepSWE and 7.06% on the hard subset of SWE-bench Pro. On DeepSWE, it outperforms the best baseline by 3.98%. Our ablation study shows that both steps of SatisFix contribute to the improvement.

papers.title: Guided Generation of Linux Kernel Semantic Patches with Small Local Language Models
papers.authors: Mohanned Ahmed
papers.summary: When a Linux kernel API changes, hundreds of drivers are converted by hand over months, and the earlier conversions are reviewed examples for the later ones. We ask whether small open language models running on a laptop can turn such examples into Coccinelle semantic patches, the rules kernel maintainers already use for tree-wide changes. We adapt guided code generation to this task: the training examples are decomposed by script into a tree of change variants, the model writes one small rule per variant under feedback from applying it to the examples, deterministic components repair SmPL syntax and generalise driver-specific names, rules are composed greedily, and a compile critic repairs or rejects a rule whose output does not build. We evaluate on a pre-registered test set of 7 migrations whose new APIs appeared after the training cutoffs of all three models (Qwen2.5-Coder 7B, Llama 3.1 8B, Gemma 3 4B), with 122 held-out driver conversions, counting a conversion as solved only if the rule's output matches the human fix and compiles. With the framework, Qwen2.5-Coder solves 35.3 conversions on average over three seeds (range 32-41), against 1.0 when prompted directly; Spinfer solves 41 and a frontier LLM agent 66. The local model solves fewer conversions than Spinfer but its rules are the most precise on the test set (0.74 of the files they change are solved, against 0.55 for Spinfer and 0.70 for the frontier agent), and the compile critic removes every output that matches the human fix but does not build. The two general-purpose models stay weak even with guidance (at most 12 solved). All code, prompts, model responses and results are released.

papers.title: Stack more levels: how to get general and human-like Mario playing
papers.authors: Shinichi Arimura, Yuchen Li, Julian Togelius
papers.summary: Super Mario Bros. is widely used in game AI and procedural content generation (PCG), yet it remains unclear whether a model-free agent can reliably win unseen levels. To address this question, we train Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) agents on increasingly large sets of PCG-generated Mario levels and evaluate their generalization on 1000 held-out test levels. We then shape competent PPO policies into three gameplay archetypes—runner, killer, and collector. Finally, we fine-tune these PPO policies using Diffusion-Reward Adversarial Imitation Learning (DRAIL) with human gameplay demonstrations. We find that increasing the number of distinct PCG-generated training levels generally improves unseen-level performance, and that fine-tuning PPO policies with DRAIL increases action-level human-likeness while preserving much of the persona induced by PPO pretraining.

papers.title: Robo-SWE: An Executable Issue-Resolution Dataset Mined from Robot Software Repositories
papers.authors: Vahid Haratian, Vahid Ansari, Mohammadhossein Malmir, Alois Knoll
papers.summary: Coding agents are evaluated mostly on general-purpose software, but domain-specific systems require domain-aware evaluation. Robot software is a particularly challenging case: Robot Operating System 2 (ROS 2) packages have their own build tools, simulators and learning frameworks are built on physics engines, and behavior that depends on timing and hardware is hard to test. We present Robo-SWE, a dataset of 236 executable issue-resolution tasks mined from merged pull requests in 28 public robotics repositories in four domains: ROS 2 systems, simulation and physics engines, robotics algorithm libraries, and robot-learning frameworks. Each task contains the original issue text, a container recipe for the repository at the commit before the fix, the developers' fix, and the developers' tests, which fail before the fix and pass after it in repeated offline runs. The dataset also keeps a provenance ledger of all 1,567 candidate pull requests, with the stage each reached and the reason for every rejection, and, as a first use, 3,540 graded attempts by five coding-agent setups with recorded patches and 3,529 available trajectories. Across three runs per primary setup, resolve rates range from 45.8% for Claude Sonnet 5.5 to 56.5% for Claude Opus 5.5; GPT-6.1 Sol reaches 54.1% at maximum effort and 52.5% at medium effort, and GPT-6 Astra 51.4%. GLM-5.3 resolves 46.2%, and Kimi K3.1 Pro 43.9%. The tasks are validated by execution; verification of their fairness by human reviewers is future work. The dataset and public leaderboard are available online.

papers.title: ADAPT: Agentic Diff-Aware Patch Testing for Pull Requests
papers.authors: Vahid Haratian, Atakan Akar, Eray Tüzün
papers.summary: Modern software development relies on pull requests (PRs) that introduce small, targeted code changes. Once merged, these changes should be protected by focused tests that exercise the behavior the PR introduces, yet developers often submit PRs without such tests, leaving the new behavior unguarded against future regressions. Most test generation techniques target entire software units and optimize objectives such as code coverage rather than the behavior a change introduces, and prior diff-aware approaches have had limited success in capturing it. We propose ADAPT (Agentic Diff-Aware Patch Testing), a regression test generation approach that uses an autonomous coding agent to produce change-focused tests for PRs. Given a PR, the agent analyzes the diff between the base and head versions to identify the modified functions and their context, then plans and generates candidate unit tests. A dedicated fail-to-pass (F2P) verification tool runs each candidate on both versions and, after F2P success, reports which executable changed lines remain uncovered; guided by this feedback, the agent iteratively refines its tests. We evaluate ADAPT on the same 426 real-world PRs used by the prior state-of-the-art baseline, with GPT-4o and GPT-5-mini. ADAPT+GPT-4o reaches an F2P rate of 62.0% (264/426), compared with BLAST's reported 35.4% (151/426), while ADAPT+GPT-5-mini reaches 89.9% (383/426). On 137 PRs shared with Change And Cover (ChaCo), ADAPT achieves full patch coverage on 83.9% of PRs, compared with 79.6% for ChaCo, at considerably lower time and cost. A manual evaluation confirms that the F2P-valid tests target each PR's intended change, with mean scores of up to 4.54/5 for importance, 4.35/5 for assertion strength, and 4.49/5 for readability, often covering behavior beyond the developer-written tests.

papers.title: Harnessing Environmental Scatterers for Endogenous Target Covertness in 6G ISAC: A New Paradigm for Sensing Security
papers.authors: Yifan Zhang, Boxuan Xie, Mingyang Yang, Ying Liu et al.
papers.summary: Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) is a cornerstone of 6G networks, enabling simultaneous data transmission and environmental perception. However, the ubiquitous radiation of sensing waveforms introduces a critical security vulnerability where the physical existence and characteristics of targets are continuously exposed to unauthorized wardens. Meanwhile, existing sensing-secure methods primarily focus on degrading a target warden's parameter-estimation accuracy, yet they fail to prevent wardens from detecting the target's physical presence. In this article, we first analyze sensing security threats in ISAC systems and survey existing sensing-secure methods. To address the critical gap, we propose a novel security paradigm termed endogenous target covertness. By intentionally harnessing environmental scatterers, such as known objects, ambient backscatter devices, and reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RIS), as ghost targets, the proposed scheme ensures a low probability that the warden detects the true target for the true target at the warden. This deliberately renders the true target's existence indistinguishable to the warden, while the legitimate base station can extract the true target's response using prior knowledge of the scatterers. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed scheme through a case study, proving that absolute target covertness can be achieved without consuming dedicated jamming power. Finally, we outline key open challenges and promising research directions to realize truly secure, ubiquitous sensing in future ISAC ecosystems.

papers.title: How Do People Debug Complex SQL Queries With LLMs? A Qualitative Study
papers.authors: Nicole Sullivan, Ella Cao, Leilani Battle, Magdalena Balazinska
papers.summary: While LLMs are increasingly used in various contexts, we lack a fundamental understanding of how they impact SQL query debugging. In response, we conducted a user study with 16 participants of varying SQL expertise, examining how they debug complex SQL queries with and without LLM support. Initial benchmarking indicated that our selected models are already capable SQL debuggers. Qualitative analyses of our study data revealed that while participants trusted the LLM, they varied widely in how and whether they delegated debugging tasks to the LLMs, which we characterized through a new three-state model of participants' SQL reasoning processes. Additionally, participants enforced specific collaborative roles for the LLM such as TA or sounding board, which participants controlled by withholding context from the LLM. These findings suggest that LLM-based tools could enable preset role selection, broader context management, and flexible automation features, including low automation options, to support SQL debugging moving forward.

papers.title: Trained on What Screen Readers Cannot Read: Accessibility Debt in the GUI Corpora Behind Computer-Use Agents
papers.authors: Obada Kraishan, Kulsawasd Jitkajornwanich
papers.summary: Computer-use agents learn to operate mobile interfaces from corpora of captured screens and accessibility trees. The same trees are what a screen reader consumes, so an agent trained on them inherits whatever labelling gaps the underlying applications carry. This paper measures one of those gaps, content-description coverage, in two Android corpora: Rico, collected in 2017, and AndroidControl, collected in 2024. Across 17,373,614 interface elements, 17.74% of the Rico elements that need a content description under our coding rule carry one, against 57.27% in AndroidControl. The difference of 39.5 percentage points holds under five alternative coding rules and when whole apps are resampled. It describes two datasets that also differ in app selection, capture method and platform version; it does not measure change over time. Input controls are the least labelled role in both corpora (2.20% and 27.21%, or 30.99% in AndroidControl if hint text counts as a name). Descriptions in the older corpus are also five times more likely to be placeholders (10.25% against 1.95%), so the difference is not an artefact of developers typing filler.
